Is the test fair to both? A difference in scores is not, by itself, evidence of unfairness: the groups may differ in vocabulary. What we can check is narrower and more useful. Take children from the two groups who do equally well on the test as a whole: do they find each item equally hard? An item on which they don't shows **differential item functioning** (DIF). [Fairness in testing](fairness.qmd) separated impact from bias; this lesson finds bias item by item. It builds the two standard methods, Mantel–Haenszel and logistic regression, takes on the question of what to match on, and applies all of it to a first-grade vocabulary test from a randomized trial, grouping the children seven demographic ways and then one more. ## Goals By the end of this lesson you should be able to: - say why a raw gap between groups mixes impact with DIF, and what matching does about it; - define uniform and non-uniform DIF with item characteristic curves, and say why DIF is always relative to the other items; - choose a matching variable, say what purifying it does, and say what robust scaling does instead; - run the Mantel–Haenszel procedure and classify items with the ETS A/B/C categories; - fit the three nested logistic-regression models for uniform and non-uniform DIF, and report an effect size; - read DIF by treatment in a randomized trial as item-to-item variation in the treatment effect. ## Core ideas ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [Fairness in testing](fairness.qmd): impact is a difference between groups in the construct itself; bias is a difference in scores that comes from something else. DIF is the item-level case of bias: an item that works differently for respondents who are equal on the construct. ::: ### DIF: the same item, at the same level of the construct ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [From the 1PL to the 4PL](1pl-to-4pl.qmd): an item characteristic curve's difficulty $b$ slides it left and right, and its slope $a$ sets how steeply it rises. Curves with different slopes cross. ::: An item shows DIF if respondents with the same $\theta$ but in different groups have different chances of answering it correctly ([Lord, 1980, "Study of item bias"](https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615-20); [AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, p. 51](https://www.testingstandards.net/open-access-files.html)). Give each group its own curve. If they differ only in $b$, one group finds the item harder at every $\theta$: **uniform DIF**. If they differ in $a$, the curves cross and the item favours one group at low $\theta$ and the other at high: **non-uniform DIF**. The group we are asking about is the **focal** group; the comparison is the **reference** group. #### An example: who recognizes which authors? The Dutch Author Recognition Test shows respondents 132 names and asks which are authors ([Brysbaert, Sui, Dirix & Hintz, 2020](https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.95); [DART_Brysbaert_2020_1](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/dart_brysbaert_2020_1/)). Its job here is intuition. Tastes in books differ by gender, which could presumably lead to some DIF: among respondents who recognize the same number of authors, do women and men recognize particular authors at different rates? Two notes on the data. Forty-two names are made-up foils, and in the IRW table a checked foil scores 1 like a recognized author, so we drop them using the paper's list. A score from the test itself: the total, the rest score (the total without the studied item), or $\theta$ estimated from the other items. The items in the matching score are the **anchor**. Two things follow. First, DIF is relative to the anchor: if every item were harder for the focal group by the same amount, the matched comparison would find nothing, since a shift common to all items looks like impact. Second, DIF items contaminate the anchor. If some items are harder for the focal group, its total understates its $\theta$, and clean items drift toward favouring it. The usual remedy is **purification**: drop the flagged items from the matching score and run the analysis again ([Holland & Thayer, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2330-8516.1986.tb00186.x); [Candell & Drasgow, 1988](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662168801200304)). Purify and they come back toward zero. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Go deeper: the anchor problem, and robust scaling **Assumptions:** two groups; a unidimensional item response model (here the 2PL) fitted in each group; some unknown subset of items has DIF. **Why an anchor is unavoidable.** Fit the 2PL separately in each group and each fit fixes its own scale (mean 0, SD 1 for $\theta$). To compare the groups we need the difference between their means, and each item gives an estimate of it: if item $i$ has no DIF, the shift in its intercept between groups, divided by its slope, is the difference in means. If *every* item shifted by the same amount, the data could not say whether the groups differ or the items do. Some items have to be assumed free of DIF (the anchor), or some other assumption has to pin down the scale. The matching score does this implicitly: it treats the whole test as the anchor. Purification refines the choice iteratively, but it starts from a contaminated total, and simulations disagree about when it helps ([Zwick, 2012, pp. 16–22](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2012.tb02290.x)). **Robust scaling.** [Halpin (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-024-09957-6) recasts DIF as outlier detection. Each item's implied estimate of the group difference is one data point; items without DIF cluster around the true difference, and DIF items are outliers. A robust estimator of the centre (a redescending M-estimator, which gives far-out items zero weight) estimates the group difference without choosing anchors in advance, and it is tuned so that items without DIF are flagged at a chosen false-positive rate. Wald tests then compare each item with that robust centre. The paper develops it for the 2PL in two independent groups. The `robustDIF` package ([Halpin, 2026](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.robustDIF)) implements it with Tukey's bisquare, taking separate `mirt` fits as input, and also tests whether ignoring DIF changes the estimated difference between groups. It is a reasonable choice when no set of items can be trusted as anchors in advance, as in a trial where the program may have moved any item. *With real data* runs it on the vocabulary test. ::: ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **If you've done** [Factor analysis II](fa-confirmatory.qmd): an unequal loading in a multigroup factor model is non-uniform DIF and an unequal intercept is uniform DIF ([Meredith, 1993](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294825)); the model estimates the factor and the group difference jointly, while the methods here match on an observed score, one item at a time. ::: ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz({ q: "Every item on a test is 0.3 logits harder for group F than for group R, at every $\\theta$. What will a DIF analysis matched on the total score find?", options: [ {text: "Essentially no DIF", correct: true, why: "A shift shared by every item looks exactly like a difference in $\\theta$. DIF is defined relative to the other items, so only departures from the common pattern show up."}, {text: "Uniform DIF against F on every item", correct: false, why: "The matched comparison sets F respondents beside R respondents with the same total; if every item shifted equally, those respondents answer each item alike."}, {text: "Non-uniform DIF, since the shift is the same size everywhere", correct: false, why: "Non-uniform DIF means the curves cross (different slopes). An equal shift in $b$ doesn't make curves cross."} ] }) ``` ### The Mantel–Haenszel procedure and the ETS categories At each total score $k$, cross group with right and wrong on the studied item. Write $A_k, B_k$ for the reference group's right and wrong answers, $C_k, D_k$ for the focal group's, and $n_k$ for everyone at that score. The common odds ratio $$\hat\alpha_{MH} = \frac{\sum_k A_k D_k / n_k}{\sum_k B_k C_k / n_k}$$ pools the tables ([Mantel & Haenszel, 1959](https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/22.4.719)); a chi-square tests whether it is 1. [Holland and Thayer (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2330-8516.1986.tb00186.x) brought it to DIF, reported on ETS's scale of item difficulty, $$\Delta_{MH} = -2.35 \ln \hat\alpha_{MH},$$ negative when the item is harder for the focal group. ETS sorts items into three categories ([Zwick, 2012, pp. 3–4](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2012.tb02290.x)): - **A** (negligible): the chi-square is not significant at .05, or $|\Delta_{MH}| < 1$; - **C** (moderate to large): $|\Delta_{MH}| \ge 1.5$ and significantly greater than 1; - **B** (slight to moderate): everything else. Needing only a matching score and counts, it is a reasonable first choice for uniform DIF in large samples. A relative standardizes the difference in proportions correct across score levels ([Dorans & Kulick, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1986.tb00255.x)). ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Go deeper: when the Mantel–Haenszel null is exact **Assumptions:** $I$ dichotomous items; the Rasch model holds in both groups with the *same* difficulties (no DIF); local independence; the groups may have any distributions of $\theta$. Matching is on the total score $r$, studied item included. ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [The Rasch model](rasch.qmd): the sum score is sufficient for $\theta$. Conditioning on it removes $\theta$: $\Pr(\mathbf{x} \mid r, \theta) = \prod_i \varepsilon_i^{x_i} / \gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)$, with $\varepsilon_i = e^{-b_i}$ and $\gamma_r$ the elementary symmetric function. ::: **The item, given the total.** Add that conditional probability over the patterns with $x_i = 1$ and total $r$. Each is item $i$ right plus $r - 1$ right among the others, so $$\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid r, \theta) = \frac{\varepsilon_i\, \gamma_{r-1}^{(i)}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)}{\gamma_r(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)},$$ where $\gamma_{r-1}^{(i)}$ is the elementary symmetric function of the other items. It contains no $\theta$. Within a score level, every respondent, whatever their $\theta$ and whichever group they belong to, has the same chance of getting item $i$ right. So in every $2 \times 2$ table the population odds ratio is exactly 1, however different the groups' $\theta$ distributions ([Holland & Thayer, 1986](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2330-8516.1986.tb00186.x); [Zwick, 1990](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986015003185)). Impact cannot pass for DIF. **Why the studied item belongs in the total.** Match on the rest score $s = r - x_i$ instead. Given $\theta$, $x_i$ is independent of the other items, so $\Pr(x_i = 1 \mid s, \theta) = \Pr(x_i = 1 \mid \theta)$: $\theta$ is back, and $s$ only partly pins it down. If the reference group's $\theta$ is higher, its members at rest score $s$ are higher on average too, and every item appears to favour it (Zwick, 1990). Including the item looks like double counting; under the Rasch model it is what makes the comparison exact. **Why the 2PL loses this.** Under the 2PL, the weighted score $\sum_i a_i x_i$ is sufficient, not $r$ ([From the 1PL to the 4PL](1pl-to-4pl.qmd)). Within a level of $r$, $\theta$ still varies with *which* items were right, and its distribution there differs between groups whose $\theta$ distributions differ. The odds ratios then drift from 1, in either direction, for items whose slopes differ from the rest. The simulation below shows it: with an impact of 1 SD, clean items are flagged more often when slopes vary than when they are equal. ::: With many items and large samples, something is nearly always significant. The categories add a size criterion, and at ETS it is the C items that go to review committees ([Zwick, 2012, p. 11](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.2333-8504.2012.tb02290.x)). A flag is a fact about an item in a sample. The *Standards* ask for a substantial explanation before an item is called biased ([AERA, APA & NCME, 2014, p. 51](https://www.testingstandards.net/open-access-files.html)), and it comes from the item's content, not the statistic. (If you've done [From construct map to items](instrument-building.qmd): the number flags the item; the text decides.) ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz({ q: "An item has $\\Delta_{MH} = -0.6$ with $p < .001$ in a sample of 20,000. Which ETS category is it, and what does that mean?", options: [ {text: "A: the difference is probably real but small, below the size ETS flags", correct: true, why: "Category A covers items that are not significant *or* have $|\\Delta| < 1$. With 20,000 respondents small differences are significant; the size rule keeps them from being flagged."}, {text: "C, because the p-value is tiny", correct: false, why: "C needs $|\\Delta| \\ge 1.5$ as well as significance. The p-value reflects the sample size as much as the size of the DIF."}, {text: "B, because it is significant and negative", correct: false, why: "B needs $|\\Delta| \\ge 1$. The sign says which group the item favours (here the reference group), not the category."} ] }) ``` ### Logistic regression DIF ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} **Recall** from [The likelihood and logistic regression](likelihood.qmd): regressing chess responses on Elo, with an intercept for each problem, is an ordinary logistic regression fitted by maximum likelihood, and comparing log likelihoods compares models. ::: The most straightforward DIF analysis is that same logistic regression, one item at a time, with the matching score as the predictor ([Swaminathan & Rogers, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1745-3984.1990.tb00754.x)). Fit three nested models for item $i$: $$\begin{aligned} M_0:&\quad \text{logit} \Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 r_j,\\ M_1:&\quad \text{logit} \Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 r_j + \beta_2 g_j,\\ M_2:&\quad \text{logit} \Pr(x_{ij} = 1) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 r_j + \beta_2 g_j + \beta_3 g_j r_j, \end{aligned}$$ with $r_j$ the matching score and $g_j = 1$ for the focal group. $M_1$ adds uniform DIF: $\beta_2$ is where the action is, the difference in log odds between groups at the same score. $M_2$ adds non-uniform DIF: $\beta_3$ lets the slope on the score differ by group. Likelihood-ratio tests compare the models in turn, or $M_0$ with $M_2$ for both kinds at once. How big is the DIF? $e^{\beta_2}$ is an odds ratio at a fixed score, like $\hat\alpha_{MH}$, so $2.35\,\beta_2$ sits on the delta scale. Or take the change in Nagelkerke's pseudo-$R^2$ from $M_0$ to $M_2$; [Jodoin and Gierl (2001)](https://doi.org/10.1207/S15324818AME1404_2) proposed categories for it, which `difR` implements as negligible below 0.035, moderate from 0.035 to 0.07 and large above ([Magis, Béland, Tuerlinckx & De Boeck, 2010](https://doi.org/10.3758/BRM.42.3.847)). Why the workhorse? It is a model we already know, fitted with `glm()`; it tests non-uniform DIF, which Mantel–Haenszel pools away; it takes continuous matching variables and extra covariates; and it extends to ordered categories as a cumulative logit model (problem 3; [Crane, Gibbons, Jolley & van Belle, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.mlr.0000245183.28384.ed)). Comparing item parameters estimated in each group is a third family ([Lord, 1980, "Study of item bias"](https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203056615-20); [Thissen, Steinberg & Wainer, 1993](https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203357811)). #### Try it: uniform and non-uniform DIF The studied item has $b = 0$ and $a = 1$ in the reference group; the sliders set its focal-group curve. Fifteen other items complete the matching score; 2,000 respondents per group, no impact. ```{ojs} //| echo: false viewof w2_b = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Focal group's difficulty"}) viewof w2_a = Inputs.range([0.4, 2.5], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "Focal group's slope"}) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ width: 700, height: 260, x: {label: "Ability θ"}, y: {label: "P(correct)", domain: [0, 1]}, color: {legend: true, domain: ["reference", "focal"], range: [palette.main, palette.contrast]}, marks: [Plot.line(grid(-4, 4).flatMap(t => [{t, p: p2pl(t, 0, 1), grp: "reference"}, {t, p: p2pl(t, w2_b, w2_a), grp: "focal"}]), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: "grp", strokeWidth: 2.5})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false w2 = { const b = Array.from({length: 16}, (_, i) => (i === 7 ? 0 : -1.5 + 3 * i / 15)); const {X, g} = simGroups({seed: 5, nPer: 2000, nItems: 16, b, dif: [{item: 7, db: w2_b, a: w2_a}]}); return {mh: mhAll(X, g)[7], lr: logisticDIF(X, g, 7)}; } md`Mantel–Haenszel delta **${w2.mh.delta.toFixed(2)}** (category ${w2.mh.ets}). Logistic regression: group coefficient **${w2.lr.group.toFixed(2)}** (times 2.35: ${(2.35 * w2.lr.group).toFixed(2)}); slope on the total score ${w2.lr.b1.toFixed(2)} in the reference group and ${(w2.lr.b1 + w2.lr.interaction).toFixed(2)} in the focal group.` ``` With the slope at 1, the delta and 2.35 times the group coefficient move together. Now set the difficulty to 0 and the slope to 2: the curves cross, the delta stays near 0, and the slopes on the total part company. Mantel–Haenszel pools over scores and can miss DIF that changes sign; the interaction term sees it. ```{ojs} //| echo: false quiz({ q: "In a logistic-regression DIF analysis, adding group to the model improves the fit a lot, but adding the group × score interaction does not. What kind of DIF is it?", options: [ {text: "Uniform: the item is harder for one group by about the same log odds at every score", correct: true, why: "The group term shifts the curve; the interaction would change its slope. Only the shift is needed."}, {text: "Non-uniform: the groups' curves cross", correct: false, why: "Crossing curves need different slopes on the score, which is the interaction term, and it didn't help."}, {text: "None: the interaction is what detects DIF", correct: false, why: "The group term alone detects uniform DIF; the interaction adds the non-uniform kind."} ] }) ``` ### Treatment as a grouping variable In a randomized trial, treatment assignment is a grouping too: among children with the same total, is an item easier for treated children? It is if the program raises some items much more than others. DIF by treatment is variation in the treatment effect from item to item ([Gilbert, Kim & Miratrix, 2023](https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986231171710); [Ahmed et al., 2025](https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2024.2361337)). It says what the effect on the total is made of. ## Simulate The code below simulates 20 2PL items for two groups, the focal group 1 SD lower on $\theta$ and items 9 and 10 harder for it by 0.6 logits, and runs Mantel–Haenszel on every item in 100 replications, matching on the total and on a purified total. It is base R and takes a few seconds. With the seed as written, the DIF items' mean delta is −1.3 (true values −1.3 and −1.4), significant in 99% of replications. On the contaminated total the clean items drift upward (mean delta 0.13) and are significant 8.7% of the time, against a nominal 5%; purified, 7.4%. Set `slopes_vary <- FALSE` and the purified rate falls to 3.6%. Try `n_dif <- 6` (33% false flags on the total), and `n_dif <- 0` with `impact <- 2`. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} #| results: markup #| warning: false #| message: false #| include: true #| label: unnamed-chunk-17 # Differential item functioning, simulated: two groups answer 20 items from a 2PL. # The focal group sits `impact` SDs below the reference group, and `n_dif` items # (from item 9 on) are harder for the focal group by `dif` logits at every theta (uniform DIF). # Each replication runs the Mantel-Haenszel procedure on every item, matching on the # total score and then on a purified total, and records which items are flagged. # Base R only; runs in a few seconds. set.seed(252) n_ref <- 1000; n_foc <- 1000 # respondents per group n_items <- 20 impact <- 1.0 # reference mean minus focal mean, in SDs of theta n_dif <- 2; dif <- 0.6 # how many DIF items, and how much harder for the focal group slopes_vary <- TRUE # FALSE: every slope 1 (the Rasch model) reps <- 100 a <- if (slopes_vary) exp(seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = n_items)) else rep(1, n_items) b <- seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = n_items) dif_items <- seq_len(n_dif) + 8 # items 9, 10, ...: middling difficulty, slope near 1 # Mantel-Haenszel delta and its chi-square p-value for one item (g = 1 is focal). mh <- function(y, g, score) { k <- score + 1; K <- max(k) A <- tabulate(k[y == 1 & g == 0], K); B <- tabulate(k[y == 0 & g == 0], K) C <- tabulate(k[y == 1 & g == 1], K); D <- tabulate(k[y == 0 & g == 1], K) n <- A + B + C + D; s <- n > 1 A <- A[s]; B <- B[s]; C <- C[s]; D <- D[s]; n <- n[s] nR <- A + B; nF <- C + D; m1 <- A + C; m0 <- B + D chisq <- max(0, abs(sum(A) - sum(nR * m1 / n)) - 0.5)^2 / sum(nR * nF * m1 * m0 / (n^2 * (n - 1))) c(delta = -2.35 * log(sum(A * D / n) / sum(B * C / n)), p = pchisq(chisq, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) } one_rep <- function() { g <- rep(0:1, c(n_ref, n_foc)) theta <- rnorm(n_ref + n_foc, mean = ifelse(g == 1, -impact, 0)) bb <- matrix(b, length(g), n_items, byrow = TRUE) bb[g == 1, dif_items] <- bb[g == 1, dif_items] + dif p <- plogis(sweep(theta - bb, 2, a, "*")) X <- matrix(rbinom(length(p), 1, p), nrow = length(g)) # Stage 1: match on the total. Stage 2: drop flagged items from the total # (each studied item stays in its own matching score) and run again. s1 <- sapply(1:n_items, function(i) mh(X[, i], g, rowSums(X))) flag <- which(s1["p", ] < 0.05 & abs(s1["delta", ]) >= 1) s2 <- sapply(1:n_items, function(i) mh(X[, i], g, rowSums(X[, union(setdiff(1:n_items, flag), i), drop = FALSE]))) rbind(delta_total = s1["delta", ], sig_total = s1["p", ] < 0.05, delta_purified = s2["delta", ], sig_purified = s2["p", ] < 0.05) } out <- replicate(reps, one_rep()) # 4 x n_items x reps clean <- setdiff(1:n_items, dif_items) summary_table <- data.frame( matching = c("total", "purified"), mean_delta_dif_items = c(mean(out["delta_total", dif_items, ]), mean(out["delta_purified", dif_items, ])), power = c(mean(out["sig_total", dif_items, ]), mean(out["sig_purified", dif_items, ])), mean_delta_clean_items = c(mean(out["delta_total", clean, ]), mean(out["delta_purified", clean, ])), type_I_error = c(mean(out["sig_total", clean, ]), mean(out["sig_purified", clean, ]))) print(summary_table, digits = 2) # The true DIF on the delta scale is -2.35 x the log odds ratio. For a 2PL item that is # about -2.35 * a * dif near the middle of the scale. round(-2.35 * a[dif_items] * dif, 2) op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1)) plot(1:n_items, rowMeans(out["delta_total", , ]), pch = 19, col = "#2780e3", ylim = c(-2.5, 1), xlab = "Item (DIF items from item 9 on)", ylab = "Mean MH delta over replications") points(1:n_items, rowMeans(out["delta_purified", , ]), pch = 1, col = "#c2410c") abline(h = c(-1, 0, 1), lty = c(3, 2, 3), col = "#999") legend("bottomright", c("matched on total", "matched on purified total"), pch = c(19, 1), col = c("#2780e3", "#c2410c"), bty = "n") par(op) ``` ::: [Download this code](code/dif-sim.R) to run it in your own R session. ## With real data Our table is [gilbert_meta_11](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/gilbert_meta_11/): a vocabulary test from a cluster-randomized trial of a content literacy program, in which treated schools taught thematic science and social studies lessons ([Kim, Relyea, Burkhauser, Scherer & Rich, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09609-6); data at [doi:10.7910/DVN/HQEMN6](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/HQEMN6)), in the trial collection of [Gilbert, Himmelsbach, Soland, Joshi & Domingue (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.70025). A positive delta favours the focal group. race <- function(g) ifelse(w[[g]] == 1, 1, ifelse(w$cov_white == 1, 0, NA)) groups <- list( "girls vs. boys" = 1 - w$cov_male, "Black vs. White" = race("cov_black"), "Hispanic vs. White" = race("cov_hispanic"), "Asian vs. White" = race("cov_asian"), "English learners vs. not" = w$cov_lep, "IEP vs. not" = w$cov_iep, "low income vs. not" = w$cov_ses_low, "treated vs. control" = w$treat) t(sapply(groups, function(g) c(focal = sum(g == 1, na.rm = TRUE), reference = sum(g == 0, na.rm = TRUE)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` focal reference girls vs. boys 1138 1209 Black vs. White 868 448 Hispanic vs. White 761 448 Asian vs. White 194 448 English learners vs. not 533 1814 IEP vs. not 188 2159 low income vs. not 941 1406 treated vs. control 1286 1061 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # The Mantel-Haenszel procedure for one item. Children are matched on a score (by # default the total on all 24 items, the studied item included); within each score # level k we have a 2 x 2 table of group by right/wrong. The common odds ratio pools # the tables; delta = -2.35 ln(alpha) puts it on the ETS delta scale (Holland & # Thayer, 1986). SE: Robins, Breslow & Greenland (1986). Chi-square: with the # continuity correction, as ETS computes it (Zwick, 2012, eq. 3). mh <- function(y, g, score) { ok <- !is.na(g) y <- y[ok]; g <- g[ok]; s <- score[ok] A <- tapply(y == 1 & g == 0, s, sum) # reference, right B <- tapply(y == 0 & g == 0, s, sum) # reference, wrong C <- tapply(y == 1 & g == 1, s, sum) # focal, right D <- tapply(y == 0 & g == 1, s, sum) # focal, wrong n <- A + B + C + D keep <- n > 1 A <- A[keep]; B <- B[keep]; C <- C[keep]; D <- D[keep]; n <- n[keep] R <- A * D / n; S <- B * C / n alpha <- sum(R) / sum(S) P <- (A + D) / n; Q <- (B + C) / n var_log <- sum(P * R) / (2 * sum(R)^2) + sum(P * S + Q * R) / (2 * sum(R) * sum(S)) + sum(Q * S) / (2 * sum(S)^2) nR <- A + B; nF <- C + D; m1 <- A + C; m0 <- B + D chisq <- max(0, abs(sum(A) - sum(nR * m1 / n)) - 0.5)^2 / sum(nR * nF * m1 * m0 / (n^2 * (n - 1))) c(delta = -2.35 * log(alpha), se = 2.35 * sqrt(var_log), chisq = chisq, p = pchisq(chisq, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)) } # The ETS categories (Zwick, 2012, pp. 3-4). A: not significant at .05, or |delta| < 1. # C: |delta| >= 1.5 and |delta| significantly greater than 1. B: everything else. ets <- function(delta, se, p) { ifelse(p >= 0.05 | abs(delta) < 1, "A", ifelse(abs(delta) >= 1.5 & (abs(delta) - 1) / se > qnorm(0.95), "C", "B")) } mh_all <- function(g, score = rowSums(X), cols = items) { out <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(cols, function(i) mh(X[, i], g, score)))) out$ets <- ets(out$delta, out$se, out$p) out } summarise_mh <- function(r) c(significant = sum(r$p < 0.05), A = sum(r$ets == "A"), B = sum(r$ets == "B"), C = sum(r$ets == "C"), largest = round(max(abs(r$delta)), 2)) ``` ::: What does no DIF look like? The effect size is the change in Nagelkerke's # R^2 from M0 to M2, classified as Jodoin & Gierl (2001) do in difR: below .035 # negligible (A), .035 to .07 moderate (B), above .07 large (C). nagelkerke <- function(m, ll0, n) { cs <- 1 - exp(2 * (ll0 - as.numeric(logLik(m))) / n) cs / (1 - exp(2 * ll0 / n)) } lr_item <- function(y, g, total) { d <- data.frame(y = y, g = g, total = total)[!is.na(g), ] ll0 <- as.numeric(logLik(glm(y ~ 1, binomial, d))) m0 <- glm(y ~ total, binomial, d) m1 <- glm(y ~ total + g, binomial, d) m2 <- glm(y ~ total * g, binomial, d) c(beta_group = unname(coef(m1)["g"]), p_uniform = anova(m0, m1, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"], p_nonuniform = anova(m1, m2, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"], p_both = anova(m0, m2, test = "LRT")[2, "Pr(>Chi)"], dR2 = nagelkerke(m2, ll0, nrow(d)) - nagelkerke(m0, ll0, nrow(d))) } lr_all <- function(g) { out <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(items, function(i) lr_item(X[, i], g, rowSums(X))))) out$jg <- ifelse(out$p_both >= 0.05 | out$dR2 < 0.035, "A", ifelse(out$dR2 < 0.07, "B", "C")) out } lr <- lapply(groups, lr_all) # Side by side with Mantel-Haenszel: items significant (2-df test), and the Jodoin & # Gierl categories. t(sapply(lr, function(r) c(significant = sum(r$p_both < 0.05), A = sum(r$jg == "A"), B = sum(r$jg == "B"), C = sum(r$jg == "C"), largest_dR2 = round(max(r$dR2), 3)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` significant A B C largest_dR2 girls vs. boys 4 24 0 0 0.008 Black vs. White 9 24 0 0 0.017 Hispanic vs. White 12 24 0 0 0.025 Asian vs. White 4 24 0 0 0.023 English learners vs. not 9 24 0 0 0.010 IEP vs. not 6 24 0 0 0.007 low income vs. not 9 24 0 0 0.014 treated vs. control 17 23 0 1 0.244 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # Treatment, item by item: the group coefficient (a log odds ratio at a fixed total; How large the program's effect on vocabulary is depends on which items we let define vocabulary. What should a trialist take from this? Two assumptions first: that the total is meant to measure vocabulary broadly, and that an effect concentrated in a few items means something different from one spread across many. Given those, my rule is to run a DIF analysis by treatment before reporting a trial's effect on a total score. Here it says that over a quarter of the raw effect is one word, which the curriculum materials may explain and a reader of the effect size would want to know. Construct a 2PL example with two groups whose $\theta$ distributions differ in which it is not. What happens under the Rasch model if you match on the rest score? 2. **Demographic DIF, with treatment held out (PS5#3).** Treated children are 62% of the low-income group and 50% of the others. Repeat the demographic analyses within the control group only. Which B items survive? How can DIF by treatment show up as DIF by a demographic grouping? 3. **Polytomous DIF on the CES-D.** [alexandrowicz_2018_cesd](https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/tables/alexandrowicz_2018_cesd/) holds the 20-item CES-D ([Radloff, 1977](https://doi.org/10.1177/014662167700100306)), answered 0–3 by a general-population sample in Austria ([Alexandrowicz, Jahn & Wancata, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0197908)). The positively worded items arrive keyed. For ordered categories, logistic regression becomes a cumulative logit model, $\text{logit} \Pr(x_{ij} \ge k) = \beta_{0k} + \beta_1 s_j + \beta_2 g_j + \beta_3 g_j s_j$, with $s_j$ the rest score ([Crane, Gibbons, Jolley & van Belle, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.mlr.0000245183.28384.ed); the `lordif` package, [Choi, Gibbons & Crane, 2011](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v039.i08)). Fit it per item with `MASS::polr`, grouping on `cov_sex` (264 of 518 in the source file are coded 2, the paper's number of women; no codebook confirms it). Which item flags most strongly, in which direction, and why might it? Compare [Cole, Kawachi, Maller & Berkman (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0895-4356(99)00151-1). (If you've done [Models for polytomous responses](polytomous.qmd): this is DIF in the category boundaries.) 4. **An anchor outside the test.** `gilbert_meta_11` also records `std_baseline`, each child's standardized score before the trial. Match on it instead of the total: cut it into ten groups and run the Mantel–Haenszel procedure by treatment. How do the deltas compare with those matched on the total, and why are they nearly all positive? What does an external matching variable assume, and what question does it answer? 5. **Design.** You are building a mathematics test for a state with many English learners. Where in development would you look for bias, and with what data? [Martiniello (2008)](https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.78.2.70783570r1111t32) combined DIF statistics with children's think-alouds; what does each tell you that the other can't? 6. **Challenge: schooled worlds.** [Kroupin et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2407955122) compared children with and without formal schooling on typical executive-function tasks, and argue that the tasks reflect culturally specific development. If such items showed DIF between these groups, would that be bias, a different construct, or both? What data could tell?
